notes.meaning: Paul urges the Corinthians to copy his way of living, just as he copies Jesus Christ. He does not ask them to follow him blindly, but only where he faithfully walks in the footsteps of Jesus. Christians are called to show Christ's love and humility in their daily actions so others can see a godly example.

Paul praises the believers in Corinth for keeping him in mind and holding onto the teachings he passed along to them. These traditions were the core Christian truths and practices delivered by the apostles, not man-made rules. Holding firmly to apostolic teaching keeps a church grounded in the truth.

Paul explains that God has set up an orderly structure of headship: Christ is the head of every man, the man is the head of woman, and God the Father is the head of Christ. In this context, being the head refers to loving authority and divine order, not one person being better or more valuable than another. Even within the Trinity, Jesus willingly submits to the Father while remaining fully equal in nature.

A man who prays or speaks God's message with his head covered brings shame upon his head. In Greek and Roman culture, men prayed with uncovered heads to show their direct accountability to Christ. Covering his head would send the wrong signal by hiding the dignity God gave him as Christ's representative.

A woman who prays or proclaims God's word with her head uncovered dishonors her head. In Corinthian culture, going without a veil was as shameful as having her head shaved like an unfaithful woman or an outcast. Paul explains that by covering her head, a woman shows modesty, proper respect, and honor for God's created order.

A man should not cover his head during worship because he directly reflects the image and glory of God in his role of leadership. The woman, in turn, reflects the glory of the man by coming alongside him as his partner and honor. Both are made in God's likeness, but each has a distinct way of reflecting God's design in the community.

Paul points back to the creation story in Genesis to explain this order. The first man did not come from the woman, but the woman was formed from the man's side to be his helper and companion. God designed this original relationship so that husband and wife would support each other in harmony.

Because of this divine order, a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, especially in the presence of the angels. Holy angels observe Christian worship and rejoice to see reverence and orderly submission to God's ways. Wearing a covering honors the spiritual order that angels themselves respect.

Paul quickly balances his teaching by reminding believers that in the Lord, men and women need each other and cannot stand alone. Even though the first woman came from man, every man since then has been born of a woman. Ultimately, all life comes from God, so neither sex has any reason to boast or look down on the other.

Paul asks the Corinthians to judge the matter for themselves using their common sense. He asks whether it is proper for a woman to pray to God in public with an uncovered head. He appeals to their shared sense of decency and good manners in that culture.

Paul appeals to the natural sense of fitness that long hair is a disgrace for a man, but an ornament and glory for a woman. God gave women naturally longer hair as a gentle covering that marks the clear difference between the sexes. Believers are called to respect the natural distinctions God created between men and women.

If anyone wants to argue about this matter, Paul notes that neither the apostles nor the wider churches of God practice any other custom. The standard among the early congregations was clear and consistent across regions. Believers are urged to maintain peace and modesty rather than starting needless arguments over church practices.

differ.view: Women should continue to wear fabric head coverings in public worship today because Paul bases his reasoning on the creation order.
Physical head coverings were a cultural expression of modesty and respect in the ancient world, so modern women do not need to wear them as long as the principle of respect remains.

notes.meaning: Paul turns to another serious problem and tells the church that he cannot praise them here. When they gather for worship, their bad behavior actually does more harm than good. Worship meetings should build believers up in love rather than tearing them apart.

Paul has heard reliable reports that there are selfish cliques and divisions when the church meets together. He notes that such clashes inevitably happen, and God uses them to make clear who is genuinely faithful and approved. Hard times and disagreements test our character and show who truly walks in love.

Because of their division and selfish behavior, their gatherings could no longer truly be called the Lord's Supper. They might have met in the same room, but their actions completely ruined the sacred purpose of the meal. The Lord's Supper is meant to show unity and mutual love, not self-indulgence.

When they sat down to eat, each person rushed ahead to consume their own food without waiting to share. Wealthy members ate lavishly and even became drunk, while poor members were left hungry and embarrassed. Their greed turned a feast of Christian love into an ugly display of selfishness.

Paul sternly asks if they lack homes where they can eat and drink their regular meals. By acting this way at church gatherings, they showed contempt for God's family and humiliated poorer brothers and sisters who had nothing to bring. Paul makes it plain that he cannot praise such shameful behavior.

Paul reminds them of the sacred teaching he received directly from the Lord and passed on to them. On the very night Jesus was betrayed by Judas, He instituted this holy meal with His disciples. Paul grounds their worship in what Jesus Himself said and did.

Jesus gave thanks, broke the bread, and told His disciples that it represents His body given for them in sacrifice. After supper, He took the cup of wine, explaining that it represents the new covenant sealed by His shed blood, and instructed them to drink it in remembrance of Him. The new covenant is God's promise to forgive our sins through the sacrifice of Jesus.

differ.view: The bread and cup are purely symbolic memorials that help believers remember Christ's death, without any physical change in the elements.
Christ is not physically in the bread and wine, but believers spiritually feed on Him and receive His grace through faith during the meal.
The true body and blood of Christ are really and bodily present in, with, and under the bread and wine.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The bread and wine undergo transubstantiation, entirely changing into the literal body, blood, soul, and divinity of Jesus Christ while keeping only the outward appearance of bread and wine.

notes.meaning: Every time Christians eat this bread and drink this cup, they publicly proclaim the saving death of Jesus to the world until He returns in glory. The Lord's Supper looks back to the cross and forward to the second coming of Christ. Taking communion is a steady, visible testimony of our faith in Jesus.

Anyone who eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner sins against the body and blood of Christ. An unworthy manner means taking communion carelessly, treating it like common food, or harboring division and unrepented sin. Believers are called to approach this sacred table with genuine reverence and thankfulness.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Being guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord implies that Christ's actual physical body and blood must be truly present in the sacrament.

notes.meaning: Before eating the bread and drinking the cup, every believer must examine their own heart and life. This means looking inside to confess sins, renew faith in Christ, and check that one's attitude toward other church members is loving. Self-examination is not meant to keep believers away, but to prepare them to partake with a clean heart.

differ.view: Self-examination ensures that communicants recognize their need for forgiveness and understand what they receive, which is why communion is shared only with those of the same confession.

notes.meaning: Anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body brings God's judgment upon themselves. This means failing to treat the sacred signs of Christ's sacrifice with proper honor, or failing to value the church as Christ's united body. Taking communion lightly invites God's fatherly correction instead of His blessing.

Paul explains that this irreverence is why many among them were physically weak and sick, and some had even died. God sent physical illness as a serious warning and chastening to wake the church up. God cares deeply about how His people treat the holy things of faith and one another.

If believers would judge and correct themselves through honest repentance, they would not need to fall under the Lord's discipline. When the Lord does discipline His children, He does so out of love to train them and protect them from eternal condemnation with the world. God's discipline is a sign of His mercy, keeping His people on the right path.

Paul concludes by telling the church to wait for one another whenever they gather for the Lord's Supper. If someone is truly hungry, they should eat at home first so their gathering does not result in God's judgment. He adds that he will give directions about any remaining details when he visits them in person.
